source.title: Scaling Laws for Pre-training Agents and World Models
source.authors: Tim Pearce; Tabish Rashid; David Bignell; Raluca Georgescu; Sam Devlin; Katja Hofmann

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some extracted figure labels are garbled, but the relevant results are also described in the text or tables.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether scaling-law patterns and compute-optimal allocations transfer from language modeling to embodied world modeling and behavior cloning, and includes small-scale language-modeling analyses.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own scaling sweeps, compute-optimal fits, an 894M-parameter extrapolation run, small-scale language-modeling experiments, and loss-to-performance correlations. The meta-analysis of prior imitation-learning results is included only for the correlations the authors calculate and report; results merely cited from other work are not recorded. Hyperparameters used to train the models are not separate findings.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own scaling sweeps and fits compute-optimal power laws for embodied world modeling and behavior cloning, which is a new setting for these laws. It also runs one extrapolation check at 894M parameters and small character- and GPT-2-token language-model sweeps on how tokenizer and loss affect the allocation exponent. Its results bear on V5, V7, V2, small-scale V3, and partly V6. The main experiments are not text pretraining, so rows on embodied systems bear on V5 and V7 rather than on the LM-specific versions.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors add that the WM-Token-256 coefficients closely match LLM (Chinchilla) values. With tokenized observations, BC should scale data much faster than model size, while BC-CNN should scale model size faster. They attribute the differences to loss sparsity, target granularity and tokenizer compression, supported by tiny language-modeling experiments. Downstream relevance is left as an open question.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts language-model scaling analyses and compute-optimal fitting methods to embodied world modeling and behavior cloning, with different datasets, tokenizers, architectures, and training objectives.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted allocation coefficients vary with task (world modeling versus behavior cloning), architecture (tokenized versus CNN), tokenizer compression and tokens per observation, and fitting method (frontier versus parametric). BC-Token saturation and fit suitability also differ from the other configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: BC-Token needs about 556x more compute per action prediction than BC-CNN at equal parameter count, which the authors give as the explanation for its late-plateauing curves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How the input encoding counts tokens per decision changes the effective compute per parameter, and with it the scaling allocation.

record.problems: The study treats training loss as a proxy for test loss rather than directly reporting held-out loss scaling. BC-Token models do not saturate in the tested compute range, requiring a parametric fit that makes assumptions about training curves. The 894M extrapolation is one run with limited hyperparameter tuning. The reported loss-to-online-return meta-analysis is based on plotted results from prior work, and downstream relevance remains open.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible separately reported results were left out.

untested.parts: There are no held-out text-LM loss power laws over several orders of magnitude. The embodied loss-versus-compute fits are recorded under V5.
Extrapolation for language models, and extrapolation over more than about one order of magnitude.
Compute-optimal allocation for LMs beyond tiny scale (under 17M parameters, about 1e15 FLOPs).
Not tested. No sweep of depth, width or shape at fixed parameter count.
Video-model pretraining as such, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes.
Downstream task performance of language models, and online return of the paper's own agents.

missing.what: Compute-optimal model sizes at 1e18 and 1e19 FLOPs: 2M and 11M for BC-Token-540 versus 27M and 110M for WM-Token-540.
Spread of the RT-1 optimal-parameter coefficient across three repeated runs per tokenizer. Rows cover only the one example set shown in Figure C.2.
Doptimal exponents for the Shakespeare experiments: 0.37 dense, 0.50 sparse, about 0.85 super-classed.

record.verdict_notes: R20-R29 (RT-1 world models) were moved from V3 to V5 and V7, because they are embodied systems, not language-model pretraining. R31 and R32 use modified objectives and now bear on V7 only. R37 was unlinked from V4 and the reader's V4 'challenges' label dropped, because the study has no depth or width comparison at fixed parameter count. Training loss is used as a proxy for test loss, justified by the infinite-data regime. Loss-exponent values (R15-R18) come from garbled figure labels. There is no uncertainty on any coefficient.

versions.untested_parts: The main experiments are embodied-agent pretraining, and the small language experiments analyze optimal allocation rather than testing held-out language-model loss power laws over several orders of magnitude.
Tests extrapolation for WM-Token-256 with one larger model; does not establish prediction across other tasks, architectures, or modalities.
Tests model-size and dataset-size allocation against compute in the reported setups, not the original LLM setups or all training regimes.
Compares selected task and architecture combinations, not a broad controlled sweep of depth, width, and architecture at fixed parameter count.

Tests image-based embodied world modeling and behavior cloning, plus small language-modeling experiments; does not test video-model pretraining, fine-tuning, transfer, or repeated-data regimes as such.
Tests pretraining-loss correlations with online return in a meta-analysis and with world-model video metrics; does not establish broad downstream-task predictability across language models.

Tests dependence on task, architecture, tokenizer compression, and fit method in the reported experiments; does not vary every parameter-counting, schedule, data-quality, or fitting choice mentioned in the version.

rows.subject: WM-Token-256, 894M-parameter run
rows.operation_detail: Train a larger model to check extrapolated compute-optimal loss, model size, and token count.

conditions.value: about an order of magnitude more than the scaling-law analyses

rows.measure: Agreement of actual run with extrapolated optimal predictions
rows.value: The authors report very good agreement at approximately 1.58 × 10^21 FLOPs.
rows.note: The authors note the 894M run's learning-rate and batch-size hyperparameters could be further optimized.
rows.check: This is embodied world modeling, not text, so it also bears on V5. The test is one run at about one order of magnitude more compute. The comparison point was chosen as the one closest to the extrapolated loss curve, so the loss match is partly built in. The authors acknowledge a gap between prediction and run and attribute it to untuned hyperparameters.

rows.subject: BC-Token-540 and BC-CNN
rows.size_stated: BC-Token uses dz + da = 556 inputs per predicted action; BC-CNN uses one input
rows.operation_detail: Compare the compute and training-curve behavior of tokenized and CNN-encoded behavior-cloning architectures.

conditions.value: tokenized observations versus one continuous CNN embedding

rows.measure: Loss-curve saturation and compute per action prediction
rows.value: The authors state that BC-Token models plateau much later; at 1M transformer parameters they estimate about 556 times more compute for BC-Token action prediction.
rows.note: This is a reported architectural comparison and explanation, not a broad controlled sweep at fixed parameter count.
rows.check: This is the authors' explanatory compute-per-prediction argument comparing input-encoding architectures across tasks. It is not a comparison of depth or width at fixed parameter count, and it reports no loss at fixed N, so it does not bear on V4. The coefficient changes it explains are already in R9 to R14.
